reads: A month ago, however, a dear friend, whom I have known for many years, has done me the honour to ask my hand in marriage
text: Helen became engaged a month ago, to a man she has known for many years.

reads: His name is Armitage—Percy Armitage—the second son of Mr. Armitage, of Crane Water, near Reading
text: Percy Armitage is the fiance, the man who cares for her but seems to doubt her fears.

reads: My stepfather has offered no opposition to the match
text: Roylott has not opposed Helen's engagement.
These are nearly the words she used of Julia's engagement. The same violent man is again calm about losing money, and last time the calm ended in a death before the wedding.

reads: Two days ago some repairs were started in the west wing of the building, and my bedroom wall has been pierced
text: Repairs began two days ago, and they have made Helen's own bedroom unusable.

reads: so that I have had to move into the chamber in which my sister died, and to sleep in the very bed in which she slept
text: Helen now sleeps in Julia's room and in Julia's bed.
I predicted that something would have changed around her recently. Two things have: an engagement a month ago, and a move into the death room two days ago.
Repairs starting soon after the engagement, and forcing her into that room, look convenient. Are they a pretext?
options: Roylott arranged the repairs to put her in Julia's room
The repairs are genuine and the move is bad luck
hindsight: She does not say who ordered the repairs or whether they were needed. A first-time reader has only the timing and the suspicion of Roylott to go on.

text: She does not say who ordered the work, what was wrong with the wall, or why she had to take that room and no other in so large a house.

reads: I suddenly heard in the silence of the night the low whistle which had been the herald of her own death
text: Last night, in Julia's room, Helen heard the same low whistle.
When Julia asked (¶37), Helen had never heard a whistle from her own room. Within about two nights of moving into Julia's room she hears it. Whatever makes it seems connected with that room.
options: The whistle can only be heard in that room
It is meant for whoever sleeps there
It is only Helen's nerves

reads: as I lay awake, thinking over her terrible fate
text: She was brooding on Julia in Julia's bed, which is just when a frightened mind might supply a whistle, and she admitted doubt about the sound at the inquest (¶52). But this time there was no gale, and she was fully awake.
Julia heard the whistle for 'the last few nights' (¶40) before she died. If the pattern holds, Helen has days at most, well short of the wedding.

reads: I sprang up and lit the lamp, but nothing was to be seen in the room
text: She did what Julia seems to have done with the match (¶54), and she saw nothing. Whatever whistled was not visibly in the room, or was not noticed in a quick look.

reads: got a dog-cart at the Crown Inn, which is opposite, and drove to Leatherhead
text: She got the dog-cart from the inn opposite the house.
This answers who took her: the cart came from the inn, presumably with an inn driver, since Holmes placed her beside one. So no one in the household need know she left, though the inn may.

reads: Yes, all.
text: Her account is finished and it contains no recent death. The black is not fresh mourning unless she has left one out: it is long grief, economy or a wish not to be noticed.

reads: You are screening your stepfather.
text: She has just said she told everything, and Holmes says she did not. Her account has at least one gap, and it is on the subject of Roylott.

reads: Miss Roylott, you have not.
text: She is Helen Stoner, not a Roylott. It looks like a slip by Holmes or by Watson as recorder, and nothing seems to follow from it.

reads: Five little livid spots, the marks of four fingers and a thumb, were printed upon the white wrist.
text: Her wrist carries the bruised print of a hand.
A hard grip can leave separate bruises from the fingers and thumb, and such marks fade within days or a couple of weeks.
exceptions: The timing varies from person to person, and the marks do not show who made them.

text: Someone seized her wrist hard, and not long ago. Holmes spotted it, and she had hidden it under the lace.

reads: He is a hard man
text: She does not dispute it. Roylott did this, so his violence reaches her personally and recently.

reads: perhaps he hardly knows his own strength
text: She excuses him even now, as she paid off the blacksmith. She is no eager accuser, so what she does say against him gains weight, but she may have softened other things too.
When did he grip her, and why? She does not say.
options: Something to do with the wedding
She had questioned or crossed him
Ordinary temper, unconnected with the danger

reads: Yet we have not a moment to lose
text: Holmes takes the danger as real and immediate, without treating the whistle as nerves.

reads: would it be possible for us to see over these rooms without the knowledge of your stepfather
text: He wants the rooms themselves, and he wants Roylott kept in the dark. He already treats the stepfather as the other side.
What to look at on the visit: whether the wall in Helen's old room really needed work, and what is different about Julia's room compared with the others.

reads: he spoke of coming into town to-day upon some most important business
text: Roylott is expected to be in London today on important business.
What important business does a recluse have in town, on the very day she has come there secretly?
options: Money or legal matters connected with the wedding
Something he needs for a further attempt
He has found out where she went
Nothing to do with her

reads: We have a housekeeper now, but she is old and foolish
text: There is now a housekeeper at the house, and Helen thinks she can be got out of the way.
'No servant would stay' was true only of the past. There is one more person in the house, though Helen does not count her as much of a witness.

reads: I shall return by the twelve o’clock train
text: The return ticket gets used, as expected. For today at least, her reason for going back is to let Holmes in while Roylott is away, but that plan was made only now and cannot explain the ticket she bought at dawn.

reads: I have myself some small business matters to attend to
text: Holmes has an errand before going down, and he has not named it. With so little time, it is probably connected with the case.
options: Checking the money, perhaps the mother's will
Some other inquiry about Roylott
Unrelated business
hindsight: Nothing says what the errand is. The guess about the will rests only on the reader's own wish to see the figures.

reads: Yet if the lady is correct in saying that the flooring and walls are sound
text: Watson rightly says 'if'. The sealed room reaches us through Helen's report of her own evidence and the coroner's search (¶56), and she has just been caught leaving something out. The room can be checked in person.
The cheetah and baboon will not do. Door, shutters and chimney would keep out a beast of that size, and Julia had no marks of violence (¶56).
Stop asking how someone got in. If nobody could enter, what could harm a woman alone in a locked room?
options: Something that was already in the room before she locked it
Something that reached her through an opening the search missed
Something acting without anything entering, such as a gas or drug
Nothing external: fear or illness
hindsight: This needs only the locked-room habit of separating 'no person entered' from 'nothing reached her'. None of the options is yet favoured by the text.

text: One small thing sits oddly with sealed, separate rooms: Julia was troubled in her room by the smell of Roylott's cigars (¶35), although the rooms have 'no communication' (¶33). It could have come by the corridor or the windows, but how smoke got there is worth asking.
hindsight: The cigars are mentioned only as the reason Julia went to Helen's room. A first-time reader must go back and set that passing detail against the room layout.

reads: What becomes, then, of these nocturnal whistles, and what of the very peculiar words of the dying woman?
text: Holmes will not let the sealed room close the matter. The whistles and the dying words are data, and any explanation has to account for them.

reads: we have every reason to believe that the doctor has an interest in preventing his stepdaughter’s marriage
text: Holmes reaches the motive I suspected, though Helen never stated it. His 'every reason' is still an inference, and the size of the sums remains unknown.

reads: one of those metal bars that secured the shutters falling back into its place
text: A scenario from Holmes's list: the doctor's gipsy friends are the 'band', they whistle at night, and they get at Julia through the window, with the bar clanging back as they leave.
options: The gipsies acted at the window on Roylott's behalf
The gipsies were only nearby, and the clang was something else

reads: the presence of a band of gipsies who are on intimate terms with this old doctor
text: When Helen offered this very reading of 'band', Holmes shook his head 'like a man who is far from being satisfied' (¶65). He may be laying out a line of inquiry here more than stating a belief.
A bar secured on the inside of a shutter cannot be worked from outside unless there is a gap to pass a tool through.
exceptions: Old shutters may warp or have such gaps, and a bar may be tampered with beforehand.

text: For a bar to fall back, the shutter must have been opened and shut from outside while it was fastened within, in a gale, and after that the bar must have been in place for the inquiry. Helen is also unsure she heard the clang at all (¶52).

reads: I cannot imagine.
text: Holmes himself cannot say what the gipsies did. His list connects suggestive items but contains no act that would kill anyone.
In detective stories, a theory aired before the scene has been examined often turns out to be a false lead.
exceptions: A convention and not a rule; sometimes the first idea is partly right.

reads: It is precisely for that reason that we are going to Stoke Moran this day.
text: Holmes admits the objections and goes to test them, so he is not committed to the theory. Spoken this early, it reads as the theory the visit will overturn.

I will stop building on the gipsies. No one can say what they did, the shutters and bars stand in the way, Julia had no marks of violence, and Holmes shows no faith in it. The spotted handkerchiefs remain an ingenious guess by Helen.

Open: what killed Julia with no wound and no poison found, what the 'speckled band' was, what makes the whistle and the clang, why Julia pointed towards the doctor's room (¶50), whether the repairs are genuine, how much the marriages cost Roylott, and what he is doing in town today.

Working picture: Roylott killed Julia to stop her marriage and is now setting up the same end for Helen, in the same room, within days. The method is the blank: it works in a sealed room, leaves no mark, and comes with a whistle. Helen probably survives, and Roylott's advertised death is still ahead.
options: Roylott uses some quiet means that reaches into the room without anyone entering
Roylott uses a drug or poison the doctors failed to detect
Julia's death was not a killing, and the whistle has an innocent cause
